facts.statement: The only known specimen of Changyuraptor was found in Early Cretaceous deposits 125 million years old in Liaoning Province, China.
facts.quote: It is known from a single fossil specimen representing the species Changyuraptor yangi, which was discovered from Early Cretaceous (125 million year old) deposits in Liaoning Province, China.

facts.statement: The genus and species Changyuraptor yangi were formally described in 2014.
facts.quote: In 2014, the specimen was described as the new genus and species Changyuraptor yangi.

facts.statement: The generic name Changyuraptor combines the Chinese words for 'long feather' with the Latin word for 'robber'.
facts.quote: The generic name of the dinosaur combines the Chinese words for "long feather", 長羽 (cháng yǔ), with Latin raptor ("robber", "seizer").

facts.statement: The specific name yangi honors the researcher Professor Yang Yandong.
facts.quote: The specific name honours researcher Professor Yang Yandong.

facts.statement: Changyuraptor is a genus of predatory dinosaurs known for having four wings.
facts.quote: Changyuraptor is a genus of "four-winged", predatory dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Changyuraptor belongs to the Microraptoria group of dromaeosaurid theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: C. yangi belongs to the group of dromaeosaurid theropod dinosaurs called the Microraptoria.

facts.statement: Changyuraptor is the largest known four-winged microraptorine, exceeding previous specimens in size by at least 60%.
facts.quote: These dimensions make Changyuraptor the largest four-winged microraptorine known, exceeding previously known specimens in size by at least 60%.

facts.statement: Changyuraptor had feathers covering its entire body, including forelimbs and hindlimbs, creating the appearance of two pairs of wings.
facts.quote: Like other microraptorines, Changyuraptor had feathers all over its body, including forelimbs and hindlimbs, which gives the appearance of having two pairs of wings.

facts.statement: The dinosaur's tail was long and feathered, with end feathers reaching up to 29.27 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The dinosaur's tail is long and feathered, with end feathers up to 29.27 cm long, equalling approximately 30% of the length of the animal's skeleton.

facts.statement: Researchers believe the elongated tail feathers helped provide softer and safer landings.
facts.quote: The elongated tail feathers are thought to have helped provide softer and safer landings.

facts.statement: Changyuraptor lived in moist temperate forests dominated by ginkgos and conifers, experiencing hot, dry summers and frosty winters.
facts.quote: Changyuraptor is thought to have existed alongside a variety of predatory and herbivorous dinosaurs of the Jehol Biota, including Yutyrannus, in moist temperate forest, primarily vegetated by ginkgos and conifers, with hot, dry summers and frosty winters.

facts.statement: Changyuraptor is classified within the family Dromaeosauridae.
Changyuraptor is classified within the subfamily Microraptorinae.
Changyuraptor lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Aptian (125.77 to 119.57 million years ago)

facts.statement: Changyuraptor and related microraptorines provide evidence that dinosaurs evolved features like feathers, hollow bones, and possibly flight before birds did.
facts.quote: Changyuraptor and other microraptorines add to the evidence that dinosaurs had evolved a host of morphological features and behaviours such as feathers, hollow bones, nesting behaviour, and possibly flight, before they evolved in birds.
